extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_short: patent litigation remedies and jury trials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating and proving remedies (willfulness, enhanced damages, attorney fees, prejudgment interest) and on managing jury trials in patent litigation, including factors courts consider and suggested trial-management techniques to improve juror comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion of counsel as factor in willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion letter from counsel is commonly cited as an important factor in determining willful infringement, but there is no rule that an opinion letter will necessarily preclude a finding of willfulness nor that lack of one will automatically mandate willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus is not on the legal correctness of the opinion but on whether the opinion was sufficient to instill a belief in the infringer that a court might reasonably hold the patent invalid, not infringed, or unenforceable. Relevant facts include when the infringer sought advice, what the infringer knew about counsel’s independence, skill, and competence, the nature and extent of the analysis performed by counsel, and what the infringer knew and concluded about the credibility, value, and reasonableness of the opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency of an opinion of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate/competent opinion should contain within its four corners a patent validity analysis properly and explicitly predicated on a review of the file histories and an infringement analysis comparing and contrasting the potentially infringing method or apparatus with the patented inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors bearing on competency include whether counsel examined the file history of the patent, whether the opinion was oral or written, whether it came from in-house or outside counsel, whether the opinion came from a patent attorney, and whether it was detailed or merely conclusory. A competent opinion may be unhelpful if the infringer did not rely on counsel’s advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors relevant to willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider additional facts beyond counsel opinions when determining willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include evidence of copying versus attempts to design around the patent, and evidence of frivolous litigation defenses versus substantial challenges to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egregiousness standard for increased (enhanced) damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The paramount determination for awarding increased damages is the egregiousness of the infringer’s conduct based on all the facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors that have been considered include: whether the infringer deliberately copied; whether the infringer, with knowledge of the patent, formed a good-faith belief the patent was invalid/not infringed/unenforceable; the infringer’s behavior as a party to the litigation; the infringer’s size and financial condition; the closeness of the case; the duration of the misconduct; whether the infringer took remedial action; the infringer’s motivation for harm; and whether the infringer attempted to conceal its misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 285 attorney fees framework (four parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit indicates four parts to section 285: (1) the case must be exceptional, (2) the district court may exercise its discretion, (3) the fees awarded must be reasonable, and (4) the fees may be awarded only to the prevailing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish an exceptional case the prevailing party must do so by clear and convincing evidence. Extraordinary circumstances include willful infringement or prolonged bad-faith litigation; when the accused prevails, inequitable conduct by the patentee can justify fees. Even if exceptional, an award is discretionary; the district court should set forth reasons when litigated and weigh factors to allocate litigation burdens fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable attorney fee calculation (lodestar and adjustments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation of a reasonable fee starts with a lodestar: the number of hours reasonably expended multiplied by a reasonable hourly rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable rate generally corresponds to prevailing rates in the relevant community; if non-local counsel was used for good reason, compare to rates in that attorney’s business location. Courts assess number of attorneys and cumulative hours. After lodestar, courts may adjust up or down considering results obtained; attorney’s normal billing rate; difficulty and novelty of the case; time and labor; loss of other business; customary fees for similar services; whether the fee was fixed or contingent; reputation, experience, and ability of counsel; fees paid to opposing counsel; and expenses and advancements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudgment interest: required elements and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudgment interest awards are ordinarily appropriate to afford a patentee full compensation and involve three elements: (1) the principal amount, (2) the interest rate, and (3) the method of accruing interest (compound or simple).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal must consist only of compensatory damages (lost profits or reasonable royalty), not enhanced damages. District courts have broad discretion on the interest rate and may apply rates higher than standard commercial rates if the patent owner affirmatively demonstrates a reason (e.g., contemporaneous investments or borrowing rates); state statutory rates have also been applied. Courts also have broad discretion to award simple or compound interest. Prejudgment interest is generally applied to damages as they would have been accrued; courts may award prejudgment interest on attorney fees if fees are awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for using juries in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Although litigants are constitutionally entitled to jury trials, patent cases pose special problems because jurors must often answer complex intellectual questions (e.g., invalidity/obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns include jurors’ ability to comprehend evidence and instructions, the risk of allowing juries to decide more than factual issues, the form of verdict, and adequate jury instructions. The duty of trial attorneys and the court is to present and structure the trial to educate jurors and give comprehensible evidence; techniques include relating material to jurors’ common experiences, using analogies, and employing teaching technologies (e.g., videos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial conferences to narrow issues and structure trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pretrial conferences to narrow the issues and structure the trial so that it unfolds logically and comprehensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court can identify issues that can be resolved by the judge or by consent of the litigants. Lawyers confident about evidence presentation might offer jury instructions at the pretrial conference. A proposed verdict form should accompany proposed jury instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation and phased trials as a tool to aid juror comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider bifurcating the trial (e.g., separating damages from liability, willfulness issues, or antitrust claims) or conducting multiple phases with the same jury to handle overlapping evidence and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation is not barred by the Seventh Amendment. Courts have both granted and denied motions to bifurcate; separation of validity/infringement from willfulness/damages with a 60–90 day hiatus is a recommended approach in some situations. Downsides include creating a piecemeal trial and potentially detracting from seeing the case as a whole. Bifurcation is most appropriate when there is a clearly separable issue that would control the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try one major issue at a time and treat patents/claims separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider trying one major issue at a time and, where appropriate, consider trying infringement and validity (and other issues) in separate sequence or considering different patents/claims/method vs apparatus separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some proposals suggested trying infringement first and validity only if infringement is found, both issues must be dealt with; the overarching goal is to eliminate invalid patents. Separating different patents, different claims of the same patent, or method claims from apparatus claims may help juror comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precharge the jury with legal and technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Precharge the jury by explaining legal and technical terms that will be used during the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining legal terms (e.g., obviousness) and technical vocabulary in advance helps jurors follow the evidence and the judge’s instructions; this is one of several techniques trial judges and counsel can use to simplify complex material for jurors.
